AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; OpenAI's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating model (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills, evaluation scenarios, evidence schema, commands and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the quality command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a quality command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a handful of validators for rules the team has already been hurt by, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency-cruiser, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. It proposes; it cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common Evidence record What a run leaves behind without anyone writing it: change and configuration revisions, kit version, each check with its status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending, overall status. Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable). Blocks on its own cause. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives) or a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended). The test of an adapter is how little is in it. coined Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when it has run repeatedly, leaves evidence each time and has a metric. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating model that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. The industrial sense (identical outputs from a fixed process) is explicitly not what is meant. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, clarification, plan and tasks. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. It is also the reason this site recommends starting with fewer controls than feel sufficient, on a few well-defined execution surfaces. adopted ashby

The connecting structure of the kit. coined Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the quality command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a quality command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a handful of validators for rules the team has already been hurt by, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency-cruiser, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. It proposes; it cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common Evidence record What a run leaves behind without anyone writing it: change and configuration revisions, kit version, each check with its status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending, overall status. Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable). Blocks on its own cause. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives) or a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended). The test of an adapter is how little is in it. coined Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when it has run repeatedly, leaves evidence each time and has a metric. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating model that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. The industrial sense (identical outputs from a fixed process) is explicitly not what is meant. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, clarification, plan and tasks. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. It is also the reason this site recommends starting with fewer controls than feel sufficient, on a few well-defined execution surfaces. adopted ashby

backend / API; data / storage Applies-to column Variant paths Each variant selects a subset of workflows glossary.html#workflow What a workflow is AI SDLC The software development lifecycle (SDLC) with AI agents doing part of the work in every phase, from intent and specification through design, build, verification, release and operation, while deterministic checks and human decisions stay where they are needed. Not to be confused with two nearby uses. First, the lifecycle for building AI and machine-learning systems themselves: data preparation, model training and evaluation, deployment and monitoring for drift, which IBM calls the AI lifecycle. Second, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC), one vendor's named methodology: AWS structures it as Inception, Construction and Operations phases in which AI proposes a plan and asks clarifying questions, and people approve. This site uses the plain term for the lifecycle and does not follow any one methodology. The term is written without a hyphen. common Harness Everything in a coding agent except the model itself: the context it reads, the tools it can call, the permissions that bound it, the checks that run on its output and the record of what it did. Böckeler's formulation is "Agent = Model + Harness". This site uses the wide sense — the whole engineering environment around the agent — rather than the narrow sense of the scaffolding around one model call. adopted bockeler-harness Harness engineering The practice of deliberately designing and maintaining the harness: what the agent can discover, what it can do, how its work is checked and when a person needs to decide. Böckeler frames it as building trust in coding agents through systematic controls; OpenAI's account describes the same work applied to one large codebase. Here it is the discipline, distinct from the artefact (Engineering Kit), the unit (workflow) and the operating model (software factory). adopted bockeler-harness Guides and sensors Böckeler's two kinds of control. Guides are feedforward: they anticipate the agent's behaviour and steer it before it acts (instructions, constitutions, skills, templates). Sensors are feedback: they observe after the agent acts and help it self-correct (tests, linters, type checkers, AI review). The site's own vocabulary uses other words, but the split runs through it: skills and constitutions are guides; validators, tests and the review skill are sensors. adopted bockeler-harness Two kinds of machinery (probabilistic and deterministic) Probabilistic machinery understands intent, explores code, proposes designs and summarises evidence; deterministic machinery compiles, runs tests, enforces dependency rules and blocks invalid builds. Böckeler draws the same line as computational controls (deterministic, fast, run by the CPU) versus inferential controls (semantic analysis, AI review, LLM-as-judge). The rule here is that final enforcement belongs with the deterministic side wherever a machine can check reliably. adapted bockeler-harness Steering loop Böckeler's name for the human practice of iteratively improving guides and sensors based on recurring agent failures. This site calls the same thing the feedback path, and enumerates its conversions: defect → test, recurring comment → rule, violated rule → gate, production failure → eval case. adopted bockeler-harness Feedback path The defined place each lesson goes. A defect becomes a regression test. A recurring review comment becomes a rule. A rule that keeps being violated becomes a deterministic gate. A production failure becomes an evaluation case. A misunderstood requirement becomes a readiness question. A repeated procedure becomes a skill. A brittle agent behaviour becomes a change to the harness. The change lands upstream of where the problem appeared. adapted bockeler-harness Harnessability The degree to which a codebase supports building a harness: typed languages, well-defined boundaries and a runnable local environment make sensors cheap to add. A runnable starting point for the agent and brownfield pre-flight analysis (workflow catalog) are the same concern. adopted bockeler-harness Harness template Böckeler's proposal for bundles of guides and sensors standardised for common service topologies. The Engineering Kit's technology profiles (validators and guidance per supported stack) are one concrete form of this idea, with a rule registry and evidence schema added underneath. adopted bockeler-harness Engineering Kit A working name, used on this site, for a versioned, installable package of the engineering environment a team wants its people and its coding agents to operate inside: rule registry, validators, skills, evaluation scenarios, evidence schema, commands and thin tool adapters, organised in four layers (shared core, technology profiles, tool adapters, project configuration). Not an industry term. coined Rule registry One entry per rule the team cares about, with an identifier, a statement, a route (gate, judgment or guidance), an owner and known gaps. Validators declare which rules they enforce, skills which rules they support, evidence which rule checks ran. The connecting structure of the kit. coined Rule route (gate / judgment / guidance) The decision, made once per rule, of how it is enforced. A gate is a deterministic check that can block. A judgment is a named person's call, recorded. Guidance shapes what the agent tries to do but enforces nothing. "An instruction asks; a gate refuses." Böckeler's regulation categories (maintainability, architecture fitness, behaviour) classify what a control regulates; the route classifies how strongly. coined Gate (deterministic gate) A check that runs on the output and can stop it: the quality command before a push, required checks on a pull request, policy rules at release. Different from an instruction because it refuses rather than asks. Architecture gates are what evolutionary-architecture practice calls fitness functions. common Deterministic floor The minimum a kit's first release needs before any skill: a quality command that runs the same way locally and in CI, a handful of validators for rules the team has already been hurt by, a rule registry and an evidence schema. Dull, and the only part that makes the rest safe. coined Validator A deterministic check tied to a rule identifier. Runs the same way locally and in CI, returns passed / failed / skipped / could_not_run, and can block a merge. Ships when it runs reliably and its failures are actionable. Böckeler's computational sensors (linters, type checks, dependency-cruiser, SAST, mutation testing) are validators. adapted bockeler-sensors Skill Guidance the agent loads on demand, tied to rule identifiers, that shapes what it tries to do without guaranteeing it. Probabilistic. Ships only with an evaluation history. In Böckeler's terms, a guide. common Review skill An agent that reads a diff against the applicable rules and produces findings tagged to rule identifiers. It proposes; it cannot block. Böckeler's inferential sensors (AI security review, modularity review) are the same kind of thing. adapted bockeler-sensors Harness evaluation (eval) A scenario that tests whether the agent and its environment behave as intended: given a spec with an unresolved access rule, does the agent stop and ask? Distinct from application tests. Repeated when prompts, skills, tools or models change. This site treats eval history as the bar for shipping a skill. common Evidence record What a run leaves behind without anyone writing it: change and configuration revisions, kit version, each check with its status and report link, agent findings, decisions pending, overall status. Its schema is fixed by the kit and is the one thing a project cannot customise. coined could_not_run A first-class result state, distinct from failed and skipped: the check was required but its prerequisite was missing (a tool absent from the runner image, an environment unavailable). Blocks on its own cause. Without it, the first broken runner quietly turns every gate it hosts into a suggestion. coined Adapter The thin binding between the kit's core and one tool: an execution surface (where the agent runs), a change host (where the pull request lives) or a pipeline runner (where checks run unattended). The test of an adapter is how little is in it. coined Mechanism versus meaning The kit supplies reusable mechanism (a test pattern, a runner, a rule identifier); the project supplies the meaning those mechanisms must preserve (which identities may export which records, which fields are excluded). A kit cannot infer product decisions because it has an authorization skill. coined Workflow One delivery decision run end to end: a trigger, inputs, an agent task, automated checks, guardrails, a human decision, outputs, feedback and an owner. A team has one when it has run repeatedly, leaves evidence each time and has a metric. coined Three roles (agent, checks, people) The agent does what is expensive for a person and tolerable to get slightly wrong. The checks do what must not be wrong. The people do what needs context the workflow cannot hold. Workflows fail when these blur: an agent treated as verifier, or people treated as checks. coined Risk tier Assigned at readiness or planning; selects which checks and which reviewers apply. The workflow definition stays the same, its cost scales with the change. A low tier never removes an applicable rule. common Failure path A defined response to an interruption: a check detects a violation, a required check cannot run, a requirement is ambiguous, an agent finding is rejected, an exception is requested. A test failure and an unavailable environment need different responses; treating either as a pass misrepresents the evidence. coined Evidence hand-off Workflows are built one at a time but read each other's records: the readiness record configures verification, the verification record feeds release readiness, the release record is what an incident review reads. Evidence carries its scope with it and expires when the revision changes. coined Software factory Not a product or a platform: the operating model that appears when enough workflows share rules, evidence and feedback, so that what production teaches changes what specification asks. The industrial sense (identical outputs from a fixed process) is explicitly not what is meant. coined Review fatigue More workflows, more evidence and more agent output landing on the same few approvers. Leading indicators: review latency, reviewer concentration, shortening comments. The answer is moving every mechanical check into a gate so reviewers see only decisions and exceptions. common Skill erosion What happens when agents do all the implementation and all the first drafts: the team stops getting the unaided repetitions that keep judgment sharp, and the factory depends on that judgment at every human decision point. common Spec-driven development Making expected behaviour and constraints explicit before implementation, in a sequence from intent through specification, clarification, plan and tasks. This site treats it as the process spine the harness wraps around, and stays neutral on which tool supplies it. adopted spec-kit Specification readiness Enough clarity to proceed responsibly, with remaining uncertainty made visible. A workflow whose trigger is a spec marked ready for planning, whose checks are structural, whose decision is the product owner's, and whose output is a readiness record later workflows read. coined Independent basis for verification If an agent generates both the implementation and its tests from the same incomplete understanding, both may share the same mistaken assumption. Verification needs something defined apart from the implementation: acceptance criteria, access rules, interface contracts, representative data, failure scenarios. coined The export example The running hypothetical: a feature that lets users export customer records. Open decisions (which records, which fields, large exports, failure, audit), an access rule (R-042 / SEC-004), a background worker with a broader query, a 50k-row load scenario, a volume-limit rule (R-017). It is the site's one worked example: a page that needs an example follows this change, so the abstractions can be checked against one story. coined Requisite variety Ashby's law: a regulator can only control a system if it has at least as much variety as the system it governs. Böckeler uses it to explain why committing to a narrow topology makes an agent easier to harness: restricting what the agent may produce shrinks the space the controls must cover. It is also the reason this site recommends starting with fewer controls than feel sufficient, on a few well-defined execution surfaces. adopted ashby
